parts.ask: P = (0 −1; −1 0) represents U: describe U fully as a single transformation
parts.ms: M1 reflection or the line; A1 reflection in y = −x; any reference to a centre of reflection is ignored (MS pp.18–19)
parts.er: Wrong answers: y = x, or a rotation; two transformations given scored nothing (ER pp.7–8)

parts.ask: V (matrix Q): rotation 240° anticlockwise about O followed by enlargement scale factor 6 about O: determine Q exactly
parts.ms: M1 rotation matrix or scaling by 6; A1 exact (MS pp.18–19)
parts.er: Sign errors despite the formula booklet; forgot ×6, or scaled only the diagonal (ER p.8)

parts.ask: U followed by V is T, matrix R: determine R
parts.ms: M1 QP order; A1 (MS pp.18–19)
parts.er: Fewer wrong-order products than before; sign slips (ER p.8)

parts.ask: W = (−2  2√3; 2√3  2): show there is a real λ such that W maps (λ, 1) to (4λ, 4), giving λ exactly
parts.final_form: λ = √3/3 (= 1/√3), shown to satisfy both equations
parts.ms: M1 matrix product set equal to (4λ, 4); A1 one correct equation; dM1 solves; A1 λ = √3/3; A1 both equations solved, or the value checked in the other (MS pp.18–20)
parts.er: Final mark most often lost: only one equation solved or checked; values stated without working; the uniqueness aspect ignored (ER p.8)

parts.ask: y² = 4ax, a > 0, focus S; l1: y = k (k > 0) meets C at P: show PS = (k² + 4a²)/(4a)
parts.ms: B1 x_P = k²/(4a); M1 PS via focus–directrix (x_P + a) or Pythagoras; A1* with an intermediate step (MS pp.21–22)
parts.er: Few used focus–directrix; the Pythagoras route was error-prone and often skipped the intermediate step (ER pp.8–9)

parts.ask: l2 passes through P and meets the directrix on the x-axis; it meets the y-axis at A: show y_A = 4a²k/(k² + 4a²)
parts.ms: B1 gradient 4ak/(k² + 4a²); M1 line through (−a, 0), x = 0; A1* (MS pp.21–22)
parts.er: Ill-defined letters for variables; otherwise better done than (a) (ER p.9)

parts.ask: l1 meets the directrix at B; area BPA : area OSP = 4k² : 1: determine a exactly
parts.ms: B1 area OSP = ½ak; M1 area BPA = ½ × BP × (k − y_A); M1 applies the ratio; dM1 solves; A1 1/4 (MS pp.21–22)
parts.er: Often omitted; wrong BP; ratio misapplied; poor manipulation of area BPA; a sketch helps (ER p.9)

parts.ask: Prove by induction that Σ_{r=1}^{n} log(2r − 1) = log((2n)!/(2ⁿ n!)) for all positive integers n
parts.final_form: induction with base case, step and conclusion
parts.ms: B1 n = 1: both sides log 1 (= 0); M1 adds log(2k + 1) to the assumed sum; M1 combines logs; M1 introduces (2k + 2)/(2k + 2) to build (2k + 2)!; A1 log((2k + 2)!/(2^(k+1)(k + 1)!)); A1 conclusion conveying "true for n = 1", "assumed true for n = k", "shown true for n = k + 1" and "hence true for all n" (MS pp.23–24)
parts.er: Hardest question (22% zero); base case careless (both sides taken as 1, not 0); wrong (k + 1)th term; the result claimed without introducing the cancelling factors; conclusion lacked the implication (ER pp.9–10)

parts.ask: Using the standard results for Σr² and Σr³, show Σ_{r=1}^{n} r²(r + 2) = (1/12)n(n + 1)(an² + bn + c) with integers a, b, c
parts.ms: B1 split into Σr³ + 2Σr²; M1 both standard results substituted; dM1 factorises to (1/12)n(n + 1)(quadratic); A1 a = 3, b = 11, c = 4 (MS p.7)
parts.er: Very well done; lost marks were mostly the last one through poor algebra; equating coefficients was error-prone (ER p.3)

parts.ms: B1 (MS p.8)
parts.er: Almost all correct (ER p.3)

parts.ask: Use algebra to determine the other 2 roots
parts.ms: M1 x² − 4x + 13 from the conjugate pair; M1 second factor 2x² + 3 by division, comparing coefficients or inspection; dM1 solves it; A1 both exact roots with i (±1.2247…i is M1A0). Calculator roots with reconstructed factors: first M1 only (MS p.8)

parts.ask: Show all 4 roots on a single Argand diagram
parts.final_form: pairs symmetric about the real axis, ±ki on the imaginary axis
parts.ms: B1 one pair correct; B1 both pairs correct relative to each other (ft (b)) (MS p.8)
parts.er: Occasionally ±ki plotted on the real axis (ER p.3)

parts.ask: xy = 9, P(3t, 3/t), t ≠ 0: use calculus to find the normal at P in the form ty − t³x = f(t)
parts.ms: B1 dy/dx by calculus (a stated m_T alone earns no B1); M1 m_N = t²; M1 straight line method; A1 f(t) = 3 − 3t⁴ seen in (a). No calculus: max 0111 from stated m_T, 0011 from stated m_N (MS p.9)
parts.er: Well known; some were thrown because f(t) had to be found rather than a given answer (ER p.3)

parts.ask: Given t = 2, determine where the normal meets H again, in simplest form
parts.ms: M1 normal at t = 2 with xy = 9 to a 3TQ (8x² − 45x − 18 = 0); dM1 solves; A1 (−3/8, −24), ignoring (6, 3/2) but A0 for any other extra point (MS p.9)
parts.er: Some gave P itself as the second point; solving in terms of t rarely sensible (ER p.4)

parts.ask: A = (−3 8; −3 k) maps triangle T to T′ with area of T′ three times that of T: determine the possible values of k
parts.ms: M1 det A = −3k + 24; M1 sets det = 3 or −3 and solves; A1 one value; A1 both, no extras (MS p.10)
parts.er: Commonly det set equal to 3 only, not ±3 (ER p.4)

parts.ask: B = (a −4; 2 3), BC = (2 5 1; 1 4 2), a constant: determine C in terms of a
parts.ms: B1 det B = 3a + 8; M1 B⁻¹ with their det; M1 B⁻¹(BC) in the correct order (wrong order M0 even if the result is right); A1 like terms collected. Alt: six simultaneous equations (MS p.10)
parts.er: Many did not see that B⁻¹ was needed; the six-equation route was often abandoned (ER p.4)

parts.ask: f(x) = x² − 6x + 3 has roots α, β: without solving, determine (α² + 1)(β² + 1)
parts.ms: B1 α + β = 6, αβ = 3; M1 expands to α²β² + α² + β² + 1; M1 α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ; A1 40 (α + β = −6 gives A0) (MS p.11)
parts.er: Ignoring "without solving" was expensive; sign errors in the sum (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Find a quadratic with roots α/(α² + 1) and β/(β² + 1), as px² + qx + r = 0 with integers
parts.final_form: integer coefficients: 40x² − 24x + 3 = 0 (this scheme also accepts p = 40, q = −24, r = 3)
parts.ms: B1 new sum as a single fraction over (α² + 1)(β² + 1); M1 value of new sum; M1 value of new product; A1 sum 3/5 or product 3/40; M1 x² − (sum)x + product; A1 integer-coefficient equation with "= 0", any integer multiple; this scheme also allows stating p = 40, q = −24, r = 3; requires all marks. Work for (a) that appears only in (b) earns no credit in (a) (MS p.11)
parts.er: Some did not reuse (a); marks lost to sign errors and not converting to integer coefficients (ER p.4)

parts.ask: z1 = 3 + 2i, z2 = 2 + 3i, z3 = a + bi: determine the exact value of |z1 + z2| (all stages shown)
parts.ms: M1 sum then Pythagoras; A1 √50 or 5√2; answer only no marks (MS p.12)
parts.er: Some did not know modulus or used |z1| + |z2| (ER p.5)

parts.ask: w = z2z3/z1: determine w in terms of a and b as x + iy
parts.ms: M1 multiply by (3 − 2i)/(3 − 2i); B1 13; dM1 collect real and imaginary parts; A1 single "i" form. Wrong placement of numbers: max 1010 or 1000 (MS p.12)
parts.er: Numbers substituted in the wrong places; the denominator 13 lost (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Given w = 4/13 + (58/13)i, determine a and b
parts.ms: M1 equates real and imaginary parts and solves with working; A1 (MS p.12)
parts.er: Calculator-only solving of the simultaneous equations lost marks (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Determine arg w in radians to 4 s.f.
parts.ms: M1 arctan(58/4); A1 1.502 only (MS p.12)
parts.er: Fraction inverted; degrees; wrong number of s.f. (ER p.5)

parts.ask: f(x) = x^(3/2) + x − 3: show f(x) = 0 has a root α in [1, 2]
parts.ms: M1 f(1) = −1, f(2) ≈ 1.83, one correct; A1 values, continuous, sign change and conclusion (MS p.13)
parts.er: Conclusions rarely sufficient, "continuous" often missing (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Starting with [1, 2], use interval bisection twice to show α lies in [1.25, 1.5]
parts.ms: M1 f(1.5); dM1 f(1.25); A1 values (awrt 0.3, −0.3/−0.4) and conclusion; [1.5, 1.25] not accepted; interpolation scores nothing (MS p.13)
parts.er: Some just re-tested the given interval instead of bisecting; conclusions missing (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Determine f′(x)
parts.ms: B1 (QP prints one total (3) for (c)(i) and (ii); the scheme splits B1 / M1A1) (MS p.13)
parts.er: Usually correct (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Using 1.375, apply Newton–Raphson once, 3 d.p.
parts.ms: M1 N–R with some working (answer only no marks unless 1.379592 seen); A1 awrt 1.380 (MS p.13)
parts.er: Some gave only a value: methods must be shown (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Use linear interpolation once on [1.25, 1.5] for a different approximation, 3 d.p.
parts.ms: M1 equation with differences (sign errors only); dM1 solves; A1 awrt 1.378 (MS p.13)
parts.er: Sign slips and algebra errors, more so with the line-equation approach (ER p.5)

parts.ask: P(2p², 4p) on y² = 8x: show Q(2/p², −4/p), p ≠ 0, lies on the parabola
parts.ms: B1* both coordinates substituted, 16/p² both sides, and "shown"/"true" (MS p.14)
parts.er: Many omitted the required minimal conclusion (ER p.5)

parts.ask: Show that the chord PQ passes through the focus
parts.final_form: focus (2, 0) and a demonstration with conclusion
parts.ms: B1 focus (2, 0); M1 gradient of PQ (2p/(p² − 1)); A1 equation of PQ; A1* substitutes x = 2 (or y = 0) with a further step and a conclusion. Alts: equal gradients PF and QF; similar triangles (MS pp.14–16)
parts.er: The final mark needed fully correct work and was not widely scored; y = mx + c raised the algebra (ER pp.5–6)

parts.ask: The tangents at P and Q meet at R: determine R in simplest form
parts.ms: M1A1 tangent gradient (1/p at P or −p at Q); M1A1 one tangent equation; M1 eliminate y, solve for x; A1 x = −2; dM1 substitute for y; A1 y = 2p − 2/p in simplest form. Calculus not required here (MS pp.16–17)
parts.er: Gradient at Q given as +p instead of −p; only precise algebra gave R in simplest form (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Prove by induction that 4ⁿ + 6n − 10 is divisible by 18 for n ∈ ℤ, n ≥ 2
parts.final_form: induction from n = 2 with step and conclusion
parts.ms: B1 f(2) = 18 with substitution (starting at f(3): max 01110; a comment on the divisibility of f(1) loses the last A1); M1 f(k + 1); M1 pf(k) + linear g(k); A1 f(k + 1) = 4f(k) + 18(2 − k); A1 conclusion with the bold minimum: true for n = 2, if true for n = k then true for n = k + 1, so true for all n (n ≥ 2). parts.er: Many tested n = 1 instead of n = 2; f(k) not brought in; 18 not shown as a factor of every term; incomplete conclusions (ER p.6)

parts.ms: M1 det M with a visible subtraction; M1 strategy to show det ≠ 0 (discriminant 4 − 16, completing the square, complex roots −1 ± i√3, or minimum); A1 reasoning about the sign and the word non-singular (MS p.7)

parts.ms: B1 (MS p.8)
parts.er: Almost universally correct (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Solve f(z) = 0 completely
parts.ms: M1 quadratic factor from the conjugate pair (or sum 10, product 41); A1 z² − 10z + 41; M1 linear factor 2z + k (inspection or division); A1 z = 1/2 stated in (b). Alts: product of roots 41/2 ÷ 41; or factor theorem with real/imaginary parts (MS pp.8–9)
parts.er: Long division was used more than expected and caused slips; some found 2z − 1 but never stated z = 1/2 in (b) (ER p.4)

parts.ask: Determine p and q
parts.ms: M1 expands (z² − 10z + 41)(2z − 1); A1 both (MS p.8)
parts.er: Arithmetic slips in p and q were fairly frequent, often via long division (ER p.4)

parts.ask: The roots form a triangle on an Argand diagram: determine its area
parts.ms: M1 ½ × 8 × (5 − their real root); A1ft 18 (MS p.8)
parts.er: Labelled "(c)" in the report: many used the origin instead of the real root as the third vertex; an answer of "18i" gained nothing (ER p.4)

parts.er: Almost always correct (ER p.6)

parts.ask: Root β in [6, 7]: using x0 = 6, apply Newton–Raphson once, 3 d.p.

parts.ms: M1 forms the equation in n from (a) and (b); dM1 simplifies to 9n² − 47n + 10 = 0 (or a 3-term cubic with no constant) and solves; solving a quartic directly without a full method not allowed; A1 n = 5 with 2/9, 0, −1 rejected (MS p.23)
